CHAPTER 1 OF 3 · CERVICAL PLEXUS BLOCKS

Anatomy: the cervical plexus

The cervical plexus is formed from the ventral rami of C1–C4, which join in three loops. The cutaneous (superficial) branches come from C2–C4; the deep branches supply the prevertebral muscles, help supply SCM, trapezius and the scalenes, and C3–C5 form the phrenic nerve.

Four cutaneous branches, one exit point

Where the branches emerge and what they supply

1
Right side
Front
The midpoint of the posterior border of SCM (Erb’s point): the four branches come round the border here, about the level of the thyroid cartilage. Superficial block site.

Schematic, not to scale. Nerve territories overlap and vary.

BRANCH	ROOTS	SUPPLIES
Lesser occipital
C2
Scalp behind and above the ear
Great auricular
C2–C3
Angle of the jaw, skin over the parotid, most of the ear and the mastoid
Transverse cervical
C2–C3 (C3–C4 in some texts)
Front of the neck
Supraclavicular
C3–C4
Lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest

The face (trigeminal nerve) and the back of the scalp (greater occipital nerve, a dorsal ramus) are not part of the cervical plexus.

Three layers, three blocks
BLOCK	WHERE THE LOCAL ANAESTHETIC GOES	WHAT IT BLOCKS
Superficial
Subcutaneous, superficial to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Cutaneous branches (sensory)
Intermediate
Between the investing layer (around SCM) and the prevertebral fascia
Cutaneous branches (sensory), more reliably
Deep
Deep to the prevertebral fascia, at the C2–C4 roots beside the transverse processes
Cutaneous and deep (motor) branches; often the phrenic nerve

Terms vary between papers: some call the intermediate block a “superficial” block. Ask which layer is meant.

Deep cervical plexus landmarks
1

Right side
C2: about 2 cm below the mastoid tip, on the line to Chassaignac’s tubercle.
C3: about 4 cm below.
C4: about 6 cm below.

The line runs from the mastoid tip to Chassaignac’s tubercle (C6), just behind the posterior border of SCM.

EXAM PEARL

For the viva

“The four cutaneous branches of C2–C4 emerge together at the midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. I block them there, superficial to the prevertebral fascia. A deep block is a paravertebral injection at the roots: it adds the motor branches and the phrenic nerve, and the risk of vertebral artery and intrathecal injection.”

CHAPTER 2 OF 3 · NECK · SUPERFICIAL AND INTERMEDIATE

Superficial and intermediate cervical plexus block

Local anaesthetic around the four cutaneous branches of C2–C4 where they come round the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The superficial block is subcutaneous; the intermediate block is deeper, between the investing and prevertebral layers of the deep cervical fascia. Sensory only, and for most indications as good as the deep block and safer.

USE IT FOR

Carotid endarterectomy (awake)
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery (both sides)
Superficial neck surgery and lymph node biopsy
Clavicle surgery (with a brachial plexus block)
POSITION
Supine or semi-sitting, head turned slightly away
PROBE
Linear, transverse over the midpoint of SCM
NEEDLE
50 mm, in-plane, lateral to medial
DOSE
5–15 ml of 0.25–0.5% ropivacaine (or 0.25% bupivacaine, 1% lidocaine)
COVERS
Skin of the anterolateral neck, the angle of the jaw and ear, behind the ear and over the clavicle (C2–C4)

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine or semi-sitting, with the head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked. Expose the neck and upper chest so you can see the length of SCM. To find its posterior border, ask the patient to lift the head off the pillow. Slide the pillow away from the hand holding the needle.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe
50 mm short-bevel needle; 10 ml syringe
5–15 ml of local anaesthetic. The plexus is purely sensory here, so a dilute solution is enough: ropivacaine 0.25–0.5%, bupivacaine 0.25% or lidocaine 1%.
Monitoring, oxygen, and the local anaesthetic toxicity kit within reach
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (superficial) technique. Find the midpoint of the posterior border of SCM (Erb’s point, about the level of the thyroid cartilage), where the four branches fan out. Insert the needle just under the skin there and inject about 3 ml, then fan 2–3 cm up and down the border with about 7 ml more, subcutaneously. Total 10–15 ml. Keep it shallow: no deeper than 1–2 cm.

Ultrasound. Probe transverse over the middle of SCM, about the level of the cricoid. Slide posteriorly until the tapering posterior edge of SCM is in the middle of the screen. Look for the interscalene groove and brachial plexus deep to the bright prevertebral fascia. The cervical plexus is a small honeycomb of hypoechoic dots just deep to the posterior edge of SCM and superficial to the prevertebral fascia. Sometimes the great auricular nerve is seen as a single dot on the surface of SCM.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial (posterior to anterior). For the intermediate block, pass through the investing fascia so the tip sits beside the plexus, under the posterior edge of SCM. If you can’t see the plexus, put the tip in the plane between SCM and the prevertebral fascia, close to the posterior border of SCM (the sub-SCM approach).

Sonoanatomy

Superficial to deep: skin, fat and platysma; SCM (wrapped in the investing layer of deep cervical fascia); fat; the prevertebral fascia; then the scalene muscles with the brachial plexus roots between them. Medially, deep to SCM: the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Sternocleidomastoid
Scalene muscles
Target and deposition

Intermediate: the fluid should layer out between SCM and the prevertebral fascia and surround the plexus. If it doesn’t, reposition and inject again. Superficial: a subcutaneous layer over the posterior border of SCM. Never inject deep to the prevertebral fascia: that is the deep block, with its risks.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

5–15 ml of 0.25–0.5% ropivacaine per side

Bupivacaine 0.25% or lidocaine 1% also work. For thyroid surgery both sides are blocked: add up the total dose.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
Moderate: usually adequate
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear
Transverse cervical (C2–C3): the front of the neck
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Supraclavicular (C3–C4): lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest

Covers: Skin of the anterolateral neck (C2–C4): angle of the jaw and most of the ear, behind the ear, the front of the neck and over the clavicle.

MECHANISM

The four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular) all come round the posterior border of SCM near its midpoint before they fan out under the skin. One injection there reaches all four.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Skin cover is reliable. It is sensory only: the deep structures of the neck (the carotid sheath, muscles, thyroid capsule) are not reliably covered, so the surgeon usually adds local infiltration, for example around the carotid sheath during endarterectomy.

WHAT IT MISSES
The face. The mental, infraorbital and supraorbital nerves are trigeminal branches, not cervical plexus. See face blocks.
The back of the neck and the occipital scalp (dorsal rami; greater occipital nerve).
Deep structures without the surgeon’s infiltration.
Complications and how to avoid them
Intravascular injection (internal jugular, carotid, external jugular): aspirate and inject in small steps. Look for the vessels with colour Doppler before you start.
Spread to the brachial plexus (an unplanned interscalene block), especially with larger volumes and higher concentrations.
Phrenic nerve block (breathlessness), Horner’s syndrome and recurrent laryngeal nerve block (hoarse voice). Rare with the superficial and intermediate blocks, but warn the patient.
Serious complications are close to zero with the superficial and intermediate blocks, and less common than with the deep block.
Practical pearls
Lifting the head off the pillow makes the posterior border of SCM easy to feel.
Look for the tapering posterior edge of SCM, not for the nerves: if the dots aren’t clear, the plane under SCM still works.
A larger volume does not mean a better block here; it means more spread to the brachial plexus and phrenic nerve.
Both sides for thyroid surgery is fine with the superficial or intermediate block. Never do a deep block on both sides.
Carotid endarterectomy under regional anaesthesia

An awake patient is the best neurological monitor while the carotid is clamped. The usual technique is a superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block plus local infiltration by the surgeon (the carotid sheath and the lower border of the mandible, where the retractor sits).

In the GALA trial (3526 patients), local and general anaesthesia gave no difference in stroke, heart attack or death at 30 days. Choose by the patient, the surgeon and the team.
In a systematic review, serious complications were more common after deep (or combined deep and superficial) blocks than after superficial or intermediate blocks, and conversion to general anaesthesia was also more frequent. The deep block is not needed for this operation.
Talk to the patient throughout and keep a plan for converting to general anaesthesia with the airway under the drapes.
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery

Bilateral superficial cervical plexus blocks give a small reduction in pain scores and opioid use after thyroid surgery. Useful as part of multimodal analgesia, not as the only technique.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

A patient is having a carotid endarterectomy under regional anaesthesia. Which block would you choose, and why not a deep cervical plexus block?

Model answer points
Superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block on the operative side, with local infiltration by the surgeon around the carotid sheath and the lower border of the mandible.
The four cutaneous branches of C2–C4 come round the posterior border of SCM at its midpoint: one injection reaches them all.
The deep block adds little for this operation and has more serious complications (vertebral artery or intrathecal injection, phrenic nerve block) and more conversions to general anaesthesia.
Awake patient = neurological monitoring during clamping. GALA: no difference in 30-day outcomes between local and general anaesthesia.
Have a plan to convert to general anaesthesia.

PRACTICE QUESTION (OSCE)

Label this ultrasound picture of the neck and show where you would put the needle tip for an intermediate cervical plexus block.

Model answer points
Sternocleidomastoid with its tapering posterior border; the investing fascia around it.
Prevertebral fascia (bright line); scalene muscles and the brachial plexus roots below it.
Internal jugular vein and common carotid artery, deep to SCM medially.
Cervical plexus: small hypoechoic dots under the posterior edge of SCM.
Tip: deep to SCM and superficial to the prevertebral fascia, next to the plexus. In-plane, lateral to medial.

CHAPTER 3 OF 3 · NECK · DEEP

Deep cervical plexus block

A paravertebral block of the C2–C4 roots as they leave the foramina: local anaesthetic deep to the prevertebral fascia, beside the transverse processes. An advanced block with a risk of serious complications, including intrathecal and vertebral artery injection. For most indications the superficial or intermediate block is as good and safer.

USE IT FOR

Rarely needed: the superficial or intermediate block covers most neck surgery
Know it for the exam and to recognise its complications
POSITION
Supine, head turned away
PROBE
Linear, transverse behind SCM at C4 (ultrasound) or landmarks
NEEDLE
50 mm, short bevel
DOSE
3–5 ml per level (C2, C3, C4), or one injection at C3 or C4
COVERS
C2–C4: the skin of the neck as for the superficial block, plus the deep muscles

Deep cervical plexus: transverse view at the C4 transverse process

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine with the head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked. Never block both sides.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (for the ultrasound technique)
50 mm short-bevel needle; extension tubing so an assistant can aspirate and inject
3–5 ml of local anaesthetic per level.
Full monitoring, oxygen, airway equipment and lipid emulsion ready before you start
Landmarks

Landmark technique. Draw a line from the tip of the mastoid process to Chassaignac’s tubercle (the C6 transverse process, felt behind the clavicular head of SCM just below the cricoid). The C2, C3 and C4 transverse processes lie on this line about 2, 4 and 6 cm below the mastoid.

Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin and advance slowly until it touches the transverse process (usually about 2 cm deep). Withdraw 1–2 mm, aspirate, and inject 3–5 ml. Three injections (C2, C3, C4), or a single injection at C3 or C4. See the landmark figure in the anatomy chapter.

Ultrasound. Transverse behind SCM. Count the levels from C6 (big anterior tubercle) or C7 (no anterior tubercle) up to C4. The root lies in the gutter between the anterior and posterior tubercles.

Needle approach

Landmark: perpendicular, to bone. Ultrasound: in-plane from posterior to anterior, onto the posterior tubercle, stopping beside the root and never medial to the tubercles.

Sonoanatomy

The transverse process looks like two bright humps (anterior and posterior tubercles) with shadows, and the round hypoechoic root between them. The vertebral artery is deep and medial, between the tubercles: always find it with colour Doppler. The phrenic nerve runs on the front of the anterior scalene, just under the prevertebral fascia.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Sternocleidomastoid
Prevertebral and scalene muscles
Target and deposition

The root, outside the intervertebral foramen, deep to the prevertebral fascia. Inject slowly in 1 ml steps after aspirating, talking to the patient.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

3–5 ml of local anaesthetic per level

Use the same agents as the superficial block. Tiny intra-arterial volumes can cause seizures: see below.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: A vertebral or carotid artery injection goes straight to the brain: 0.5 ml or less can cause a seizure. Aspirate, inject 1 ml at a time, and keep the total within the maximum.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear
Transverse cervical (C2–C3): the front of the neck
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Supraclavicular (C3–C4): lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest

Covers: C2–C4: the skin of the neck (as the superficial block) plus the deep muscles of the neck.

MECHANISM

A paravertebral injection at the C2–C4 roots, so it blocks both the cutaneous branches and the deep (motor) branches to the prevertebral muscles, SCM, trapezius and the scalenes.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense when it works. The extra depth of block over the superficial technique rarely matters for surgery.

WHAT IT MISSES
The face (trigeminal nerve).
The back of the neck and the occipital scalp (dorsal rami).
Complications and how to avoid them
Vertebral or carotid artery injection and seizures; internal jugular puncture.
Epidural or intrathecal injection: high or total spinal anaesthesia.
Phrenic nerve palsy (common with the deep block): dangerous in patients with lung disease. Never do it on both sides.
Recurrent laryngeal, hypoglossal, vagus nerve and brachial plexus block; Horner’s syndrome.
Conversion to general anaesthesia in about 2.5% of carotid endarterectomies.
Practical pearls
Bone first: touch the transverse process before injecting, then come back 1–2 mm.
Stay lateral: the vertebral artery and the foramen are medial to the tubercles.
If you are tempted to do a deep block for carotid surgery, do an intermediate block and ask the surgeon to infiltrate instead.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Describe the landmarks for a deep cervical plexus block. What are its complications?

Model answer points
Line from the mastoid tip to Chassaignac’s tubercle (C6). C2, C3 and C4 transverse processes about 2, 4 and 6 cm below the mastoid.
Needle perpendicular to bone (about 2 cm), withdraw 1–2 mm, aspirate, 3–5 ml per level.
Complications: vertebral artery injection and seizures; epidural or intrathecal spread (total spinal); phrenic nerve palsy (never bilateral); recurrent laryngeal nerve, Horner’s, brachial plexus.
Superficial or intermediate block is as good for most indications and safer.

CHAPTER 2 OF 3 · NECK · SUPERFICIAL AND INTERMEDIATE

Superficial and intermediate cervical plexus block

Local anaesthetic around the four cutaneous branches of C2–C4 where they come round the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The superficial block is subcutaneous; the intermediate block is deeper, between the investing and prevertebral layers of the deep cervical fascia. Sensory only, and for most indications as good as the deep block and safer.

USE IT FOR

Carotid endarterectomy (awake)
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery (both sides)
Superficial neck surgery and lymph node biopsy
Clavicle surgery (with a brachial plexus block)
POSITION
Supine or semi-sitting, head turned slightly away
PROBE
Linear, transverse over the midpoint of SCM
NEEDLE
50 mm, in-plane, lateral to medial
DOSE
5–15 ml of 0.25–0.5% ropivacaine (or 0.25% bupivacaine, 1% lidocaine)
COVERS
Skin of the anterolateral neck, the angle of the jaw and ear, behind the ear and over the clavicle (C2–C4)

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine or semi-sitting, with the head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked. Expose the neck and upper chest so you can see the length of SCM. To find its posterior border, ask the patient to lift the head off the pillow. Slide the pillow away from the hand holding the needle.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe
50 mm short-bevel needle; 10 ml syringe
5–15 ml of local anaesthetic. The plexus is purely sensory here, so a dilute solution is enough: ropivacaine 0.25–0.5%, bupivacaine 0.25% or lidocaine 1%.
Monitoring, oxygen, and the local anaesthetic toxicity kit within reach
Landmarks and scanning

Landmark (superficial) technique. Find the midpoint of the posterior border of SCM (Erb’s point, about the level of the thyroid cartilage), where the four branches fan out. Insert the needle just under the skin there and inject about 3 ml, then fan 2–3 cm up and down the border with about 7 ml more, subcutaneously. Total 10–15 ml. Keep it shallow: no deeper than 1–2 cm.

Ultrasound. Probe transverse over the middle of SCM, about the level of the cricoid. Slide posteriorly until the tapering posterior edge of SCM is in the middle of the screen. Look for the interscalene groove and brachial plexus deep to the bright prevertebral fascia. The cervical plexus is a small honeycomb of hypoechoic dots just deep to the posterior edge of SCM and superficial to the prevertebral fascia. Sometimes the great auricular nerve is seen as a single dot on the surface of SCM.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial (posterior to anterior). For the intermediate block, pass through the investing fascia so the tip sits beside the plexus, under the posterior edge of SCM. If you can’t see the plexus, put the tip in the plane between SCM and the prevertebral fascia, close to the posterior border of SCM (the sub-SCM approach).

Sonoanatomy

Superficial to deep: skin, fat and platysma; SCM (wrapped in the investing layer of deep cervical fascia); fat; the prevertebral fascia; then the scalene muscles with the brachial plexus roots between them. Medially, deep to SCM: the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Sternocleidomastoid
Scalene muscles
Target and deposition

Intermediate: the fluid should layer out between SCM and the prevertebral fascia and surround the plexus. If it doesn’t, reposition and inject again. Superficial: a subcutaneous layer over the posterior border of SCM. Never inject deep to the prevertebral fascia: that is the deep block, with its risks.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

5–15 ml of 0.25–0.5% ropivacaine per side

Bupivacaine 0.25% or lidocaine 1% also work. For thyroid surgery both sides are blocked: add up the total dose.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
Moderate: usually adequate
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear
Transverse cervical (C2–C3): the front of the neck
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Supraclavicular (C3–C4): lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest

Covers: Skin of the anterolateral neck (C2–C4): angle of the jaw and most of the ear, behind the ear, the front of the neck and over the clavicle.

MECHANISM

The four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular) all come round the posterior border of SCM near its midpoint before they fan out under the skin. One injection there reaches all four.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Skin cover is reliable. It is sensory only: the deep structures of the neck (the carotid sheath, muscles, thyroid capsule) are not reliably covered, so the surgeon usually adds local infiltration, for example around the carotid sheath during endarterectomy.

WHAT IT MISSES
The face. The mental, infraorbital and supraorbital nerves are trigeminal branches, not cervical plexus. See face blocks.
The back of the neck and the occipital scalp (dorsal rami; greater occipital nerve).
Deep structures without the surgeon’s infiltration.
Complications and how to avoid them
Intravascular injection (internal jugular, carotid, external jugular): aspirate and inject in small steps. Look for the vessels with colour Doppler before you start.
Spread to the brachial plexus (an unplanned interscalene block), especially with larger volumes and higher concentrations.
Phrenic nerve block (breathlessness), Horner’s syndrome and recurrent laryngeal nerve block (hoarse voice). Rare with the superficial and intermediate blocks, but warn the patient.
Serious complications are close to zero with the superficial and intermediate blocks, and less common than with the deep block.
Practical pearls
Lifting the head off the pillow makes the posterior border of SCM easy to feel.
Look for the tapering posterior edge of SCM, not for the nerves: if the dots aren’t clear, the plane under SCM still works.
A larger volume does not mean a better block here; it means more spread to the brachial plexus and phrenic nerve.
Both sides for thyroid surgery is fine with the superficial or intermediate block. Never do a deep block on both sides.
Carotid endarterectomy under regional anaesthesia

An awake patient is the best neurological monitor while the carotid is clamped. The usual technique is a superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block plus local infiltration by the surgeon (the carotid sheath and the lower border of the mandible, where the retractor sits).

In the GALA trial (3526 patients), local and general anaesthesia gave no difference in stroke, heart attack or death at 30 days. Choose by the patient, the surgeon and the team.
In a systematic review, serious complications were more common after deep (or combined deep and superficial) blocks than after superficial or intermediate blocks, and conversion to general anaesthesia was also more frequent. The deep block is not needed for this operation.
Talk to the patient throughout and keep a plan for converting to general anaesthesia with the airway under the drapes.
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery

Bilateral superficial cervical plexus blocks give a small reduction in pain scores and opioid use after thyroid surgery. Useful as part of multimodal analgesia, not as the only technique.

Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

A patient is having a carotid endarterectomy under regional anaesthesia. Which block would you choose, and why not a deep cervical plexus block?

Model answer points
Superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block on the operative side, with local infiltration by the surgeon around the carotid sheath and the lower border of the mandible.
The four cutaneous branches of C2–C4 come round the posterior border of SCM at its midpoint: one injection reaches them all.
The deep block adds little for this operation and has more serious complications (vertebral artery or intrathecal injection, phrenic nerve block) and more conversions to general anaesthesia.
Awake patient = neurological monitoring during clamping. GALA: no difference in 30-day outcomes between local and general anaesthesia.
Have a plan to convert to general anaesthesia.

PRACTICE QUESTION (OSCE)

Label this ultrasound picture of the neck and show where you would put the needle tip for an intermediate cervical plexus block.

Model answer points
Sternocleidomastoid with its tapering posterior border; the investing fascia around it.
Prevertebral fascia (bright line); scalene muscles and the brachial plexus roots below it.
Internal jugular vein and common carotid artery, deep to SCM medially.
Cervical plexus: small hypoechoic dots under the posterior edge of SCM.
Tip: deep to SCM and superficial to the prevertebral fascia, next to the plexus. In-plane, lateral to medial.

CHAPTER 3 OF 3 · NECK · DEEP

Deep cervical plexus block

A paravertebral block of the C2–C4 roots as they leave the foramina: local anaesthetic deep to the prevertebral fascia, beside the transverse processes. An advanced block with a risk of serious complications, including intrathecal and vertebral artery injection. For most indications the superficial or intermediate block is as good and safer.

USE IT FOR

Rarely needed: the superficial or intermediate block covers most neck surgery
Know it for the exam and to recognise its complications
POSITION
Supine, head turned away
PROBE
Linear, transverse behind SCM at C4 (ultrasound) or landmarks
NEEDLE
50 mm, short bevel
DOSE
3–5 ml per level (C2, C3, C4), or one injection at C3 or C4
COVERS
C2–C4: the skin of the neck as for the superficial block, plus the deep muscles

Deep cervical plexus: transverse view at the C4 transverse process

Simulated image drawn by this page, not a patient scan. Use the arrow keys on the image to step through.

Position

Supine with the head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked. Never block both sides.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (for the ultrasound technique)
50 mm short-bevel needle; extension tubing so an assistant can aspirate and inject
3–5 ml of local anaesthetic per level.
Full monitoring, oxygen, airway equipment and lipid emulsion ready before you start
Landmarks

Landmark technique. Draw a line from the tip of the mastoid process to Chassaignac’s tubercle (the C6 transverse process, felt behind the clavicular head of SCM just below the cricoid). The C2, C3 and C4 transverse processes lie on this line about 2, 4 and 6 cm below the mastoid.

Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin and advance slowly until it touches the transverse process (usually about 2 cm deep). Withdraw 1–2 mm, aspirate, and inject 3–5 ml. Three injections (C2, C3, C4), or a single injection at C3 or C4. See the landmark figure in the anatomy chapter.

Ultrasound. Transverse behind SCM. Count the levels from C6 (big anterior tubercle) or C7 (no anterior tubercle) up to C4. The root lies in the gutter between the anterior and posterior tubercles.

Needle approach

Landmark: perpendicular, to bone. Ultrasound: in-plane from posterior to anterior, onto the posterior tubercle, stopping beside the root and never medial to the tubercles.

Sonoanatomy

The transverse process looks like two bright humps (anterior and posterior tubercles) with shadows, and the round hypoechoic root between them. The vertebral artery is deep and medial, between the tubercles: always find it with colour Doppler. The phrenic nerve runs on the front of the anterior scalene, just under the prevertebral fascia.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
Sternocleidomastoid
Prevertebral and scalene muscles
Target and deposition

The root, outside the intervertebral foramen, deep to the prevertebral fascia. Inject slowly in 1 ml steps after aspirating, talking to the patient.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

3–5 ml of local anaesthetic per level

Use the same agents as the superficial block. Tiny intra-arterial volumes can cause seizures: see below.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: A vertebral or carotid artery injection goes straight to the brain: 0.5 ml or less can cause a seizure. Aspirate, inject 1 ml at a time, and keep the total within the maximum.

Coverage

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear
Transverse cervical (C2–C3): the front of the neck
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Supraclavicular (C3–C4): lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest

Covers: C2–C4: the skin of the neck (as the superficial block) plus the deep muscles of the neck.

MECHANISM

A paravertebral injection at the C2–C4 roots, so it blocks both the cutaneous branches and the deep (motor) branches to the prevertebral muscles, SCM, trapezius and the scalenes.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense when it works. The extra depth of block over the superficial technique rarely matters for surgery.

WHAT IT MISSES
The face (trigeminal nerve).
The back of the neck and the occipital scalp (dorsal rami).
Complications and how to avoid them
Vertebral or carotid artery injection and seizures; internal jugular puncture.
Epidural or intrathecal injection: high or total spinal anaesthesia.
Phrenic nerve palsy (common with the deep block): dangerous in patients with lung disease. Never do it on both sides.
Recurrent laryngeal, hypoglossal, vagus nerve and brachial plexus block; Horner’s syndrome.
Conversion to general anaesthesia in about 2.5% of carotid endarterectomies.
Practical pearls
Bone first: touch the transverse process before injecting, then come back 1–2 mm.
Stay lateral: the vertebral artery and the foramen are medial to the tubercles.
If you are tempted to do a deep block for carotid surgery, do an intermediate block and ask the surgeon to infiltrate instead.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION (VIVA)

Describe the landmarks for a deep cervical plexus block. What are its complications?

Model answer points
Line from the mastoid tip to Chassaignac’s tubercle (C6). C2, C3 and C4 transverse processes about 2, 4 and 6 cm below the mastoid.
Needle perpendicular to bone (about 2 cm), withdraw 1–2 mm, aspirate, 3–5 ml per level.
Complications: vertebral artery injection and seizures; epidural or intrathecal spread (total spinal); phrenic nerve palsy (never bilateral); recurrent laryngeal nerve, Horner’s, brachial plexus.
Superficial or intermediate block is as good for most indications and safer.

From the skin down: fat and platysma, SCM tapering laterally, then fat and the bright prevertebral fascia over the scalene muscles and the brachial plexus roots. STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Probe transverse just behind the posterior border of SCM, at the level of the upper thyroid cartilage. Slide up or down to count levels: C6 has a big anterior tubercle (Chassaignac’s), C7 has none. Then come back up to C4.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

The transverse process: anterior and posterior tubercles as two bright humps with shadows, and the C4 root in the gutter between them. Over it: the bright prevertebral fascia. Find the vertebral artery (deep, between the tubercles) and the carotid with colour Doppler before you start.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, posterior to anterior, aiming for the posterior tubercle. The tip passes through the prevertebral fascia (a click) and stops beside the root, outside the foramen. Never advance medially past the tubercles.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then inject slowly in 1 ml steps, watching for symptoms. The fluid spreads around the root under the prevertebral fascia. Stop at once if the patient feels unwell, the voice changes or the fluid is not seen.
